extracted.intended_audience: physiologists, biophysicists, and scientifically literate members of the American Association for the Advancement of Science (late 19th-century audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly lecture describing how to investigate and explain 'the life-question' by testing physiological functions, applying physical and chemical laws, and quantifying mental and bodily processes. Emphasizes experimental methods and theoretical criteria for judging whether phenomena are 'vital' or explicable by physics/chemistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: life as physiological phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'life' is used in science in the physiological sense: 'the conception represents simply the sum of the phenomena exhibited by a living being.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish metaphysical (mind/soul) and physiological senses; use the physiological sense for scientific investigation and define life operationally as the totality of observable phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of vitality (Kiiss's formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Life ... is all that can not be explained by chemistry or physics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test each separate operation in the organism—if it can be explained by chemistry or physics, then it is non-vital. The physiological investigator should therefore attempt to reproduce or account for functions by physical/chemical mechanisms before invoking a special 'vital' principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: investigate special functions to approach the life-question
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress on the life-question has been chiefly gained by investigation of special functions; physiological investigators should test separate operations in the organism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect quantitative and qualitative relations of functions, use effective experimental appliances, and accumulate collateral facts that constrain general conclusions about life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of energy applies to organisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The living organism has been brought absolutely within the action of the law of the Conservation of Energy: all its energy comes from without and is transformed, not created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain animal work/heat in terms of absorbed/stored food energy (e.g., Lavoisier's calorimeter results). Use calorimetry and measures like CO2 production to account for work and heat output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muscle action follows mechanical and measurable laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Muscles show absolute obedience to mechanical law; the work a muscle does occurs in contracting and is accompanied by loss of electric tension, evolution of heat, and CO2 production with acidification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measurements of electrical tension, heat, and gas exchange to characterize muscular work; treat muscle as a physical machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of structural and functional analogies (muscle ↔ electric organ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogies in structure and mechanism between striated muscle and the electric organ of fishes (e.g., torpedo) provide evidence about the electrical aspects of muscle action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare histological organization, reflex behavior, effects of nerve-section, pharmacological paralysers (curare), tetanus induction, and electrical stimulation to infer common mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret intermittent muscular phenomena (susurrus) as electrical discharges
rubrics_metrics.description: The susurrus or muscular sound (intermittent discharge) and tetanus frequency evidence indicate that muscular excitation occurs in discrete acts analogous to electrical discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ sensitive myographs and timing measurements (frequency thresholds, coalescence of stimuli) to infer the nature of excitatory events and their temporal summation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate origin of electric charge in muscle with physical-contact theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Electric charge in muscle may originate from purely physical causes such as contact of heterogeneous substances in tissue, in analogy to Volta/Thomson contact electricity and thermo-electric effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore contact and thermo-electric phenomena (Peltier effect, contact potentials) and consider energy balances and heat flow at interfaces as possible causes of bioelectricity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate mechanistic theories by empirical phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple theories (e.g., Marey's heat-elasticity model vs. Radcliffe's condenser/charge model of contraction) exist, judge them by their ability to explain observed phenomena like rigor mortis, relaxation under current flow, loss of contraction with blood access, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer theories that account for a wide range of facts; use experimental tests that probe predicted correlates (electrical charge patterns, mechanical behavior under thermal or electrical manipulation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproduce 'vital' processes ex vivo to test non-vital explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many functions once deemed 'vital' (digestion, absorption, respiration, circulation, coagulation) have been reproduced or explained by chemical/physical processes outside the living body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt to replicate physiological processes in vitro (e.g., chemical digestion with ferments, osmotic absorption, chemical coagulation via proteid interactions or ferments) to determine whether a special vital principle is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nervous system as electrical conductor of energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Nerve-cells and fibers function in reception and transmission of energy likely electrical; nerve elements have measurable surface tension (e.g., one-tenth of a volt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study nerve structure/composition (protagon, etc.), measure bioelectric potentials and conduction, and use comparisons to muscle to elucidate mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain slow nerve propagation using electrostatic capacity and resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent slowness of nervous transmission is not proof against electrical nature because transmission time depends on conductor capacity and resistance and scales with length (time ∝ length^2 in certain regimes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use electrical models (resistance, capacitance) and controlled experiments (vary conductor length and measure transmission time) before rejecting an electrical hypothesis for nerve transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify mental operations by measurable timing experiments (Donders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental operations are not instantaneous; use chronographic measurement (noemotachograph/noemnotachometer) to separate physiological time from recognition and volition (example: simple thought ≈ 1/25 second).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments with baseline physiological response times and subtract to obtain recognition/decision/volition durations; use controlled stimuli and counterbalanced tasks to isolate cognitive components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure mental 'energy' by blood consumption using plethysmography
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of nervous (mental) action may be measured by the quantity of blood consumed in its performance; plethysmograph recordings show increased cerebral blood flow during mental effort or imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ plethysmograph apparatus to quantify organ volume/blood flow changes during cognitive tasks (e.g., mental arithmetic, reading familiar vs. unfamiliar texts), and interpret curve changes as indices of effort; note sensitivity to dreaming and emotional stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat thought as a measurable physical force
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought can be measured, at least in rate of action and relative energy, analogous to other forms of energy by the effects produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate cognitive measurements (timing, blood consumption) to energetic frameworks; argue for physiologically grounded psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply thermodynamics to biological energy transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the law of dissipation of energy (entropy considerations) to explain that biological energy transformations are unidirectionally dissipative, producing heat as an inevitable result of incomplete conversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model muscle/organism as machines converting chemical food energy to work with concomitant heat production; use thermochemical data to quantify inefficiencies and heat evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate modern thermo-chemistry into metabolic explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Thermo-chemistry shows that chemical unions may absorb or evolve heat; metabolic pathways involve many stages each with thermal consequences, explaining the heat evolved by organisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze metabolic sequences thermodynamically (synthesis vs decomposition/exchange), and account for heat absorbed/evolved at each step when explaining organismal energy budgets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider capillarity and interfacial electricity as contributors to biological energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Capillarity is an electrical phenomenon (Draper, Lippmann); electrified curved liquid surfaces change form and can do work; osmose and imbibition (capillary phenomena) produce electricity and heat in organisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine capillary/electrocapillary effects at liquid interfaces and membranes in tissues as potential sources or mediators of biological energy; use capillary electrometers and analogous devices to detect such effects.
